verses.zh: 大祭司就说：「这些事果然有吗？」
verses.en: Then the high priest said, “Are these things true?”[NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “If it is so concerning these things” (see BDAG 422 s.v. ἔχω 10.a for this use).
verses.commentary: 7:1 "The high priest" At this time it was Caiaphas. See note at Acts 4:6.

verses.zh: 司提反说：「诸位父兄请听！当日我们的祖宗亚伯拉罕在美索不达米亚还未住哈兰的时候，荣耀的　神向他显现，
verses.en: So he replied,[NOTE:1] “Brothers and fathers, listen to me. The God of glory appeared to our forefather[NOTE:2] Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he settled in Haran,
notes: Grk “said.”
Or “ancestor”; Grk “father.”
verses.commentary:
7:2 "And he said" Stephen's defense is very similar to the theology of the book of Hebrews. He answered
the charges in two ways:

- the Jewish people had continually rejected Moses in the past

- the temple was only one of several ways that God used to speak with Israel

This is a direct answer to the charges brought against him in Acts 6:13.

▣ "Hear me" This is the AORIST ACTIVE IMPERATIVE form of the Greek word
akouō. It is used in the Septuagint to translate the famous prayer of Judaism, the
Shema (cf. Deut. 6:4-5). It is also used in the prophets to reflect the sense of "hear so
as to respond" (cf. Micah 1:2; 6:1). It is difficult to be certain this technical connotation is
present when these Jewish men express their Hebrew thoughts in Koine Greek words, but in some
contexts like this it may be true.

Remember, these early Jewish believers were Hebrew thinkers communicating in Koine Greek.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEMA

▣ "brethren and fathers" Stephen is acknowledging the presence of other Jewish leaders by
the term "brothers" and members of the Sanhedrin (called "the Council") called "Fathers."

▣ "'The God of glory" This God of glory (cf. Ps. 29:3) appeared to the Patriarch Abraham
(cf. Gen. 12:1, 15:1,4; 17:1; 18:1, 22:1), thus beginning the Jewish people.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (kabod, OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEKINAH

▣ "Abraham" Abraham was considered the father of the Jewish people. He was the first Patriarch.
His call and subsequent walk with God are described in Gen. 12:1-25:11. In Galatians 3 and later
Romans 4 Paul uses him as the paradigm of justification by grace through faith.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

▣ "when he was in Mesopotamia before he lived in Haran" Genesis 11:31 implies that Abraham
was in the city of Haran when YHWH spoke to him. However, the time of God's contact with Abraham was not
specifically stated. Abraham was from the city of Ur of the Chaldeans (cf. Gen. 11:28,31), but later moved to Haran
(cf. Gen. 11:31,32; 29:4) following God's command. The theological point is that God spoke to Abraham outside of the
land of Canaan. Abraham did not own or possess any part of the Holy Land (cf. Acts 7:5) during his
lifetime (except a cave to bury his family, cf. Gen. 23:9).

The term "Mesopotamia" (lit. "between the rivers") can refer to the different ethnic groups:

- a people group in the northern area of the Tigris and Euphrates (i.e., "Syria between the Rivers")

- a people group near the mouth of the Tigris and Euphrates (old Babylon)

verses.zh: 对他说：『你要离开本地和亲族，往我所要指示你的地方去。』
verses.en: and said to him, ‘Go out from your country and from your relatives, and come to the land I will show you.’[NOTE:1]
notes: A quotation from Gen 12:1.
verses.commentary:
7:3 "Leave your country and your relatives, and come into the land that I will
show you" This is a quote from Gen. 12:1. The theological issue involved in this quote is when
God says this to Abram:

- while he was in Ur before he took his father Terah and nephew Lot to Haran

- while he was in Haran and he waited until his father died to follow God south to Canaan

verses.zh: 他就离开迦勒底人之地，住在哈兰。他父亲死了以后，　神使他从那里搬到你们现在所住之地。
verses.en: Then he went out from the country of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. After his father died, God[NOTE:1] made him move[NOTE:2] to this country where you now live.
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The translation “made him move” for the verb μετοικίζω (metoikizō) is given by L&N 85.83. The verb has the idea of “resettling” someone (BDAG 643 s.v.); see v. 43, where it reappears.
verses.commentary:
7:4 "he left the land of the Chaldeans" Chaldea (BDB 505) may be the name of a district close to
the mouth of the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers (see note at Acts 7:2). It later came to refer to the nation
which developed in this region, also known as Babylon (BDB 93). This nation also produced many scholars
who developed mathematical formulas related to the movement of the night lights (i.e., planets, stars,
comets, etc.). This group of wise men (i.e., astrologers) was also known by the name Chaldean
(cf. Dan. 2:2; 4:7; 5:7-11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

▣ "Haran" Haran (BDB 357) is a city to which Terah, Abraham, and Lot moved (cf. Gen. 11:31-32).
Another of Abram's brothers settled there and the place is called by his name (i.e., city of Nahor,
cf. Gen. 24:10; 27:43). This city on the upper part of the Euphrates (i.e., tributary river, Balikh) was
started in the third millennium B.C. and has retained its name until today. Just as a note
of interest, Abraham's brother, Haran (BDB 248), is not spelled the same in Hebrew as the city.

▣ "after his father died" Many have seen a contradiction here between Gen. 11:26,32 and 12:4.
There are at least two possible solutions.

- Abraham might not have been the oldest son, but the most famous son (i.e., listed first).

- The Samaritan Pentateuch has Terah's age at death at 145, not 205, as the Hebrew text.

See Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, p. 378.

verses.zh: 在这地方，　神并没有给他产业，连立足之地也没有给他；但应许要将这地赐给他和他的后裔为业；那时他还没有儿子。
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] did not give any of it to him for an inheritance,[NOTE:2] not even a foot of ground,[NOTE:3] yet God[NOTE:4] promised to give it to him as his possession, and to his descendants after him,[NOTE:5] even though Abraham[NOTE:6] as yet had no child.
notes: Grk “And he.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.

Grk “He did not give him an inheritance in it.” This could be understood to mean that God did not give something else to Abraham as an inheritance while he was living there. The point of the text is that God did not give any of the land to him as an inheritance, and the translation makes this clear.
Grk “a step of a foot” (cf. Deut 2:5).
Grk “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
An allusion to Gen 12:7; 13:15; 15:2, 18; 17:8; 24:7; 48:4. On the theological importance of the promise and to his descendants after him, see Rom 4 and Gal 3.
Grk “he”; the referent (Abraham) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
7:5 "He promised that He would give it to him as a possession, and to his
descendants after him" This is an allusion to Gen. 12:7 or 17:8. The theological key is not
only God's promise, but Abraham's faith in God giving him a descendant as well as a land. This faith is
highlighted in Gen. 15:6 (cf. Gal. 3:6; Romans 4:3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

verses.zh: 神说：『他的后裔必寄居外邦，那里的人要叫他们作奴仆，苦待他们四百年。』
verses.en: But God spoke as follows: ‘Your[NOTE:1] descendants will be foreigners[NOTE:2] in a foreign country, whose citizens will enslave them and mistreat them for 400 years.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “that his”; the discourse switches from indirect to direct with the following verbs. For consistency the entire quotation is treated as second person direct discourse in the translation.
Or “will be strangers,” that is, one who lives as a noncitizen of a foreign country.
A quotation from Gen 15:13. Exod 12:40 specifies the sojourn as 430 years.
verses.commentary:
7:6 This predictive prophecy states Israel will be enslaved 400 years in Gen. 15:13,14. However,
Exod. 12:40 has "430 years" instead of "400 years." The Septuagint (LXX) translates Exod. 12:40 as
"and the sojourning of the children of Israel, while they sojourned in the land of Egypt and the land
of Canaan was 430 years."

- The rabbis have said that the number "400 years" starts with the offering of Isaac in Genesis 22.

- John Calvin has called the 400 years a round number.

- It may relate to four generations of 100 years each (cf. Gen. 15:16).

verses.zh: 神又说：『使他们作奴仆的那国，我要惩罚。以后他们要出来，在这地方事奉我。』
verses.en: But I will punish[NOTE:1] the nation they serve as slaves,’ said God, ‘and after these things they will come out of there[NOTE:2] and worship[NOTE:3] me in this place.’[NOTE:4]
notes: BDAG 568 s.v. κρίνω 5.b.α states, “Oft. the emphasis is unmistakably laid upon that which follows the Divine Judge’s verdict, upon the condemnation or punishment: condemn, punish…Ac 7:7 (Gen 15:14).”
The words “of there” are not in the Greek text, but are implied.sn A quotation from Gen 15:14.
Or “and serve,” but with religious/cultic overtones (BDAG 587 s.v. λατρεύω).
An allusion to Exod 3:12.
verses.commentary:
7:7 "And whatever nation" This is a quote from the Septuagint of
Gen. 15:14. This is not meant to be obtuse, but is a general statement. The nation was obviously Egypt.
Other nations, however (i.e., Philistia, Syria, Assyria, Babylon), would become Israel's oppressors and
God will judge them also.

▣ "and after that" This full phrase is a quote from Exod. 3:12.
Stephen is reciting a loose, running history of Israel.

This text asserts that Canaan and Jerusalem will uniquely become YHWH's special place.
This fits the emphasis of Deuteronomy (i.e., "to a land that I will show you").

▣ "in this place" In the context of the quote from Exod. 3:12,
this refers to Mt. Sinai, which is also outside the Promised Land and is the site of one of the major
events in the life of Israel (the giving of the Law to Moses, cf. Exodus 19-20).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LOCATION OF MOUNT SINAI

verses.zh: 神又赐他割礼的约。于是亚伯拉罕生了以撒，第八日给他行了割礼。以撒生雅各；雅各生十二位先祖。
verses.en: Then God[NOTE:1] gave Abraham[NOTE:2] the covenant[NOTE:3] of circumcision, and so he became the father of Isaac and circumcised him when he was eight days old,[NOTE:4] and Isaac became the father of[NOTE:5] Jacob, and Jacob of the 12 patriarchs.[NOTE:6]
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “him”; the referent (Abraham) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
God gave…the covenant. Note how the covenant of promise came before Abraham’s entry into the land and before the building of the temple.

Grk “circumcised him on the eighth day,” but many modern readers will not understand that this procedure was done on the eighth day after birth. The temporal clause “when he was eight days old” conveys this idea more clearly. See Gen 17:11-12.

The words “became the father of” are not in the Greek text due to an ellipsis, but must be supplied for the English translation. The ellipsis picks up the verb from the previous clause describing how Abraham fathered Isaac.
The twelve patriarchs refers to the twelve sons of Jacob, the famous ancestors of the Jewish race (see Gen 35:23-26).
verses.commentary:
7:8 "covenant" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "circumcision" This was practiced by all of Israel's neighbors, except the Philistines
(Greek Aegean people). For most cultures it was usually a rite of passage into manhood, but not for
Israel, where it was an initiation rite into the covenant People. It was a sign of a special faith
relationship with YHWH (cf. Gen. 17:9-14). Each Patriarch circumcised his own sons (i.e., acted as
priest for his own family). Robert Girdlestone, Synonyms of the Old Testament, p. 214, says
the rite of circumcision connected the rite of blood-shedding with the act of circumcision. Blood was
connected to

- covenant forming rites (cf. Gen. 15:17)

- covenant breaking (cf. Gen. 2:17)

- covenant redemption (cf. Isaiah 53)

▣ "the twelve patriarchs" This usually refers to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, but here it
refers to Jacob's twelve sons, who will become the tribes of Israel.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT
PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

verses.zh: 「先祖嫉妒约瑟，把他卖到埃及去；　神却与他同在，
verses.en: The[NOTE:1] patriarchs, because they were jealous of Joseph, sold[NOTE:2] him into Egypt. But[NOTE:3] God was with him,
notes: Grk “And the.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
The meaning “sell” for the middle voice of ἀποδίδωμι (apodidōmi) is given by BDAG 110 s.v. 5.a. See Gen 37:12-36, esp. v. 28.
Though the Greek term here is καί (kai), in context this remark is clearly contrastive: Despite the malicious act, God was present and protected Joseph.
verses.commentary:
7:9 "Joseph" This account is found in Gen. 37:11,28; 45:4. Stephen is trying to show that the
Jewish people and their leaders have often rejected God's chosen leader (cf. Moses in Acts 7:35).

verses.zh: 救他脱离一切苦难，又使他在埃及王法老面前得恩典，有智慧。法老就派他作埃及国的宰相兼管全家。
verses.en: and rescued him from all his troubles, and granted him favor and wisdom in the presence of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made[NOTE:1] him ruler over Egypt and over all his household.
notes: Or “appointed.” See Gen 41:41-43.
verses.commentary: 7:10 This account is found in Gen. 39:21; 41:40-46; see notes online.

verses.zh: 后来埃及和迦南全地遭遇饥荒，大受艰难，我们的祖宗就绝了粮。
verses.en: Then a famine occurred throughout[NOTE:1] Egypt and Canaan, causing[NOTE:2] great suffering, and our[NOTE:3] ancestors[NOTE:4] could not find food.
notes: Grk “came upon all Egypt.”
Grk “and,” but logically causal.

Our. Stephen spoke of “our” ancestors (Grk “fathers”) in an inclusive sense throughout the speech until his rebuke in v. 51, where the nation does what “your” ancestors did, at which point an exclusive pronoun is used. This serves to emphasize the rebuke.
Or “forefathers”; Grk “fathers.”
verses.commentary: 7:11 This account is found in Gen. 41:54-55; 42:5, see notes online.

verses.zh: 雅各听见在埃及有粮，就打发我们的祖宗初次往那里去。
verses.en: So when Jacob heard that there was grain[NOTE:1] in Egypt, he sent our ancestors[NOTE:2] there[NOTE:3] the first time.
notes: Or possibly “food,” since in a number of extrabiblical contexts the phrase σιτία καὶ ποτά (sitia kai pota) means “food and drink,” where solid food is contrasted with liquid nourishment (L&N 3.42).
Or “forefathers”; Grk “fathers.”
The word “there” is not in the Greek text. Direct objects were often omitted in Greek when clear from the context, but must be supplied for the modern English reader.
verses.commentary: 7:12 This account is found in Gen. 42:4; see notes online.

verses.zh: 第二次约瑟与弟兄们相认，他的亲族也被法老知道了。
verses.en: On their second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers again, and Joseph’s family[NOTE:1] became known to Pharaoh.
notes: BDAG 194 s.v. γένος 2. gives “family, relatives” here; another alternative is “race” (see v. 19).
verses.commentary: 7:13 This account is found in Gen. 45:1-4; see notes online.

verses.zh: 约瑟就打发弟兄请父亲雅各和全家七十五个人都来。
verses.en: So Joseph sent a message[NOTE:1] and invited[NOTE:2] his father Jacob and all his relatives to come, seventy-five people[NOTE:3] in all.
notes: The words “a message” are not in the Greek text, but are implied.
Or “Joseph had his father summoned” (BDAG 121 s.v. ἀποστέλλω 2.b).
Grk “souls” (here an idiom for the whole person).
verses.commentary:
7:14 "seventy-five persons" This follows the Septuagint (LXX) and the Dead Sea Scrolls (DSS; 4QExa)
manuscripts, while the Masoretic Text (MT) has "seventy" (cf. Gen. 46:27; Exod. 1:5; Deut. 10:22). At first this seems like a
manuscript problem between the LXX, which Stephen quotes, and the Hebrew text of Exod. 1:5. On further
reflection it may be two ways of counting all the descendants of Jacob. The problem arises between
Gen. 46:26 and 27:

- the MT of verse 27 has two sons born to Joseph in Egypt, while the LXX has nine, which means
that Ephraim and Manassah later had more children between them

- in the Hebrew text Jacob and his wife are counted, but Ephraim and Manasseh's extra children
are not counted

In the Greek text (LXX) Jacob and his wife are not counted, but the extra children of
Ephraim and Manasseh are counted. Both are accurate, but they add up the descendants in different ways at
different times in Jacob's life. The Hebrew texts known as the Dead Sea Scrolls also have "seventy-five
persons" in Gen. 46:27 and Exod. 1:5. Philo of Alexandia was familiar with both numbers.

We are all the benefactors of modern scholarship when it comes to difficult texts or
number problems like this one. There is a new type of biblical resource available today which targets
these difficult texts. I recommend:

- Hard Sayings of the Bible, IVP

- More Hard Sayings of the Bible, IVP

- Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties by Gleason Archer

- Answers to Questions by F. F. Bruce

- The Lost World of Scripture, by John Walton and D. Brent Sandy

For a discussion of Acts 7:14-15 see #1 pp. 521-522.

verses.zh: 于是雅各下了埃及，后来他和我们的祖宗都死在那里；
verses.en: So Jacob went down to Egypt and died there,[NOTE:1] along with our ancestors,[NOTE:2]
notes: The word “there” is not in the Greek text. Direct objects were often omitted in Greek when clear from the context, but must be supplied for the modern English reader.
Or “forefathers”; Grk “fathers.”
verses.commentary: 7:15 This account is found in Gen. 46:5; 49:33; Exod. 1:6.

verses.zh: 又被带到示剑，葬于亚伯拉罕在示剑用银子从哈抹子孙买来的坟墓里。
verses.en: and their bones[NOTE:1] were later moved to Shechem and placed in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a certain sum of money[NOTE:2] from the sons of Hamor in Shechem.[NOTE:3]
notes: “and they.”
See Gen 49:29-32.
Grk “But as the time for the fulfillment of the promise drew near that God had declared to Abraham.” The order of the clauses has been rearranged to improve English style. See vv. 6-7 above.
verses.commentary:
7:16 "to Shechem" There seems to be a discrepancy in Stephen's sermon from the Genesis accounts of

- the burial of Joseph recorded in Josh. 24:32

- the burial of Jacob recorded in Gen. 50:13

The problem is (1) the city; it should be Hebron, not Shechem, or (2) the patriarch; it
should be Jacob, not Abraham. However, Abraham and Jacob both bought land (cf. Gen. 23:16; 33:19). At
Hebron both Sarah and Abraham were buried (cf. Gen. 23:19; 25:9), as were Isaac and Rebekah (cf. Gen. 49:29-31)
and Jacob (cf. Gen. 50:13). Although it is uncertain about a burial plot at Shechem, it is possible that
Abraham had earlier purchased a field on his stop there in Gen. 12:6-7. Later Jacob redeemed that same
piece of land (cf. Gen. 33:19; Josh. 24:32). This is obviously speculation, but Stephen appears to be
very knowledgeable of the OT history and this would be the only way to reconcile the various accounts.

verses.zh: 「及至　神应许亚伯拉罕的日期将到，以色列民在埃及兴盛众多，
verses.en: “But as the time drew near for God to fulfill the promise he had declared to Abraham,[NOTE:1] the people increased greatly in number[NOTE:2] in Egypt,
notes: Grk “the people increased and multiplied.”

Or simply “did not know.” However, in this context the point is that the new king knew nothing about Joseph, not whether he had known him personally (which is the way “did not know Joseph” could be understood).
verses.commentary: 7:17 This would refer to Gen. 15:12-16 (the Promise) and Exod. 1:7 (their large number).

verses.zh: 直到有不晓得约瑟的新王兴起。
verses.en: until another king who did not know about[NOTE:1] Joseph ruled[NOTE:2] over Egypt.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “arose,” but in this context it clearly refers to a king assuming power.
A quotation from Exod 1:8.
According to L&N 88.147 it is also possible to translate κατασοφισάμενος (katasophisamenos) as “took advantage by clever words” or “persuaded by sweet talk.”
verses.commentary:
7:18 "until there arose another king" This is a quote from Exod. 1:8.
There has been and continues to be debate among scholars on the date of the Exodus. The identity of this
Egyptian king is caught up in the disagreement. One could identify him as an Egyptian king

- from the XVIII dynasty (1445 B.C.)

- from the XIX dynasty (1290 B.C.)

- to relate this Egyptian king to the first native Egyptian dynasty who overthrew the Hyksos (Semitic) rulers
of Egypt. This would explain the use of heteros in Acts 7:18. A native Egyptian would not want
Semites, like the Hebrews, in large numbers in his territory, fearing another invasion like the Hyksos.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DATE OF THE EXODUS

verses.zh: 他用诡计待我们的宗族，苦害我们的祖宗，叫他们丢弃婴孩，使婴孩不能存活。
verses.en: This was the one who exploited[NOTE:1] our people[NOTE:2] and was cruel to our ancestors,[NOTE:3] forcing them to abandon[NOTE:4] their infants so they would die.[NOTE:5]
notes: Or “race.”
Or “forefathers”; Grk “fathers.”
Or “expose” (BDAG 303 s.v. ἔκθετος).
Grk “so that they could not be kept alive,” but in this context the phrase may be translated either “so that they would not continue to live,” or “so that they would die” (L&N 23.89).
Or “was well-formed before God,” or “was well-pleasing to God” (BDAG 145 s.v. ἀστεῖος suggests the meaning is more like “well-bred” as far as God was concerned; see Exod 2:2).
verses.commentary: 7:19 This account is found in Exod. 1:10ff; see notes online.

verses.zh: 那时，摩西生下来，俊美非凡，在他父亲家里抚养了三个月。
verses.en: At that time Moses was born, and he was beautiful[NOTE:1] to God. For[NOTE:2] three months he was brought up in his father’s house,
notes: Grk “who was brought up for three months.” The continuation of the sentence as a relative clause is awkward in English, so a new sentence was started in the translation by changing the relative pronoun to a regular pronoun (“he”).
Or “exposed” (see v. 19).
verses.commentary:
7:20 "Moses was born" This account is found in Exodus 2; see notes online.

▣ "was lovely in the sight of God" This is a Hebrew idiom of beauty (cf. Exod. 2:2). Even
Josephus comments on Moses' beauty (cf. Antiq. 2.9.6). It must have been well known Jewish tradition.

verses.zh: 他被丢弃的时候，法老的女儿拾了去，养为自己的儿子。
verses.en: and when he had been abandoned,[NOTE:1] Pharaoh’s daughter adopted[NOTE:2] him and brought him up[NOTE:3] as her own son.
notes: Grk “Pharaoh’s daughter took him up for herself.” According to BDAG 64 s.v. ἀναιρέω, “The pap. exx. involve exposed children taken up and reared as slaves…The rendering ‘adopt’ lacks philological precision and can be used only in a loose sense (as NRSV), esp. when Gr-Rom. terminology relating to adoption procedures is taken into account.” In this instance both the immediate context and the OT account (Exod 2:3-10) do support the normal sense of the English word “adopt,” although it should not be understood to refer to a technical, legal event.
Or “and reared him” (BDAG 74 s.v. ἀνατρέφω b).
Or “instructed.”
verses.commentary:
7:21 This account is found in Exod. 2:5-6,10; see notes online.

▣ "he had been set outside" This is the Greek term ektithēmi, which means
"to expose" (cf. Acts 7:19) or "place outside." The Egyptians forced the Hebrews to abandon their
male children to the elements and wild beasts so as to control their rapid population growth.

NASB, NKJV
"Pharaoh's daughter took him away"

NRSV, NJB, REB
"Pharaoh's daughter adopted him"

TEV
"the king's daughter adopted him"

Peshitta
"Pharaoh's daughter found him"

The term anaireō literally means "to lift up." Moses was literally
"lifted up" out of the Nile River and by this act, became the adopted son of one of Pharaoh's daughters.

verses.zh: 摩西学了埃及人一切的学问，说话行事都有才能。
verses.en: So Moses was trained[NOTE:1] in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was powerful[NOTE:2] in his words and deeds.
notes: Or “was able” (BDAG 264 s.v. δυνατός 1.b.α).
Grk “heart.”
verses.commentary:
7:22 Moses had the best academic and military training (so says Josephus) available in his day at the
court of Pharaoh. Moses was a highly educated man.

▣ "he was a man of power in words and deeds" This must be a summary of Moses' later life
because at his encounter with YHWH at the burning bush he claimed he could not speak well (cf. Exod. 4:10-17).

verses.zh: 「他将到四十岁，心中起意去看望他的弟兄以色列人；
verses.en: But when he was about forty years old, it entered his mind[NOTE:1] to visit his fellow countrymen[NOTE:2] the Israelites.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “brothers.” The translation “compatriot” is given by BDAG 18-19 s.v. ἀδελφός 2.b.
Grk “the sons of Israel.”
Grk “And when.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.

7:23-24 This account is in Exod. 2:11-12; see notes online.

7:23 "he was approaching the age of forty" I think it was D. L. Moody who said Moses' life can be
divided into three groups of forty:

- for the first forty years he thought he was somebody (i.e., educated at Pharaoh's court)

- for the second forty years he thought he had become a nobody (i.e., exiled to the land of Midian because
he killed an Egyptian, and learned the ways and terrain of the Sinai desert)

- for the third forty years he found out what God could do with a nobody (i.e., led the
people of YHWH to the Promised Land)

verses.zh: 到了那里，见他们一个人受冤屈，就护庇他，为那受欺压的人报仇，打死了那埃及人。
verses.en: When[NOTE:1] he saw one of them being hurt unfairly,[NOTE:2] Moses[NOTE:3] came to his defense[NOTE:4] and avenged the person who was mistreated by striking down the Egyptian.
notes: “Hurt unfairly” conveys a better sense of the seriousness of the offense against the Israelite than “treated unfairly,” which can sometimes refer to slight offenses, or “wronged,” which can refer to offenses that do not involve personal violence, as this one probably did.
Grk “he”; the referent (Moses) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “he defended,” “he retaliated” (BDAG 55 s.v. ἀμύνομαι).
Grk “his brothers.”

verses.zh: 他以为弟兄必明白　神是藉他的手搭救他们；他们却不明白。
verses.en: He thought his own people[NOTE:1] would understand that God was delivering them[NOTE:2] through him,[NOTE:3] but they did not understand.[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “was granting them deliverance.” The narrator explains that this act pictured what Moses could do for his people.
Grk “by his hand,” where the hand is a metaphor for the entire person.

They did not understand. Here is the theme of the speech. The people did not understand what God was doing through those he chose. They made the same mistake with Joseph at first. See Acts 3:17; 13:27. There is good precedent for this kind of challenging review of history in the ancient scriptures: Ps 106:6-46; Ezek 20; and Neh 9:6-38.
Grk “he”; the referent (Moses) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary:
7:25 This verse is Stephen's assumptions (possibly Jewish traditions); it is not stated in Exodus. However, this is the
theme of Stephen's message. God's people did not seek, know, or obey Him!

verses.zh: 第二天，遇见两个以色列人争斗，就劝他们和睦，说：『你们二位是弟兄，为甚么彼此欺负呢？』
verses.en: The next day Moses[NOTE:1] saw two men[NOTE:2] fighting and tried to make peace between[NOTE:3] them, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers; why are you hurting one another?’
notes: Grk “saw them”; the context makes clear that two individuals were involved (v. 27).
Or “tried to reconcile” (BDAG 964-65 s.v. συναλλάσσω).
Or “repudiated Moses,” “rejected Moses” (BDAG 126-27 s.v. ἀπωθέω 2).
verses.commentary: 7:26-29 This account is found in Exod. 2:13-14; see notes online.

verses.en: But the man who was unfairly hurting his neighbor pushed[NOTE:1] Moses[NOTE:2] aside, saying, ‘Who made[NOTE:3] you a ruler and judge over us?
notes: Grk “him”; the referent (Moses) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “appointed.”

The Greek construction anticipates a negative reply which is indicated in the translation by the ‘tag’ at the end, “do you?” sn A quotation from Exod 2:14. Even though a negative reply was expected, the question still frightened Moses enough to flee because he knew his deed had become known. This understanding is based on the Greek text, not the Hebrew of the original setting. Yet the negative here expresses the fact that Moses did not want to kill the other man. Once again the people have badly misunderstood the situation.

verses.zh: 摩西听见这话就逃走了，寄居于米甸；在那里生了两个儿子。
verses.en: When the man said this,[NOTE:1] Moses fled and became a foreigner[NOTE:2] in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons.
notes: Or “resident alien.” Traditionally πάροικος (paroikos) has been translated “stranger” or “alien,” but the level of specificity employed with “foreigner” or “resident alien” is now necessary in contemporary English because a “stranger” is a person not acquainted with someone, while an “alien” can suggest science fiction imagery.

Grk “And after.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and contemporary English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
verses.commentary:
7:29 "At this remark Moses fled" This account is found in Exod. 2:15,22.
Moses' fear at killing an Egyptian shows that Pharaoh was not supportive of his being an adopted child
of one of his daughters. Even so, Hebrews 11:27 is clear!

▣ "and became an alien in the land of Midian" God appeared to Moses
at the burning bush in the land of Midian (cf. Exodus 3-4) and revealed His law to him at Sinai in the
land of Midian (cf. Exodus 19-20), which shows that God was not limited as to where
He revealed Himself. This same emphasis on God revealing Himself apart from the temple in Jerusalem is
seen in Acts 7:36, 44, 48, and 53.

▣ "became the father of two sons" This account is found in Exod. 2:22; 4:20; 18:3-4; see notes online.

verses.en: When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight, and when he approached to investigate, there came the voice of the Lord,

verses.zh: 『我是你列祖的　神，就是亚伯拉罕的　神，以撒的　神，雅各的　神。』摩西战战兢兢，不敢观看。
verses.en: ‘I am the God of your forefathers,[NOTE:1] the God of Abraham, Isaac,[NOTE:2] and Jacob.’[NOTE:3] Moses began to tremble and did not dare to look more closely.[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “and Isaac,” but καί (kai) has not been translated since English normally uses a coordinating conjunction only between the last two elements in a series of three or more.
A quotation from Exod 3:6. The phrase suggests the God of promise, the God of the nation.
Or “to investigate,” “to contemplate” (BDAG 522 s.v. κατανοέω 2).
A quotation from Exod 3:5. The phrase holy ground points to the fact that God is not limited to a particular locale. The place where he is active in revealing himself is a holy place.
verses.commentary:
7:32 This account is found in Exod. 3:6; see notes online.

▣ "fathers" In both the Hebrew text and Greek translation (i.e., Septuagint) the word
is SINGULAR. In every other occurrence of the phrase it is PLURAL. The
implication is that God knew Moses' slave father.

verses.zh: 主对他说：『把你脚上的鞋脱下来，因为你所站之地是圣地。
verses.en: But the Lord said to him, ‘Take the sandals off your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.[NOTE:1]
notes: Or “mistreatment.”
verses.commentary:
7:33 This account is found in Exod. 3:5. Moses approached the bush out of curiosity, not
religious devotion.

The exact reason for taking off his shoes is uncertain.

- shoes might be polluted (i.e., animal dung)

- taking off shoes might be a sign of intimacy or familiarity (i.e., at home)

- a cultural practice of the Patriarchs or Egyptian ritual

verses.zh: 我的百姓在埃及所受的困苦，我实在看见了，他们悲叹的声音，我也听见了。我下来要救他们。你来！我要差你往埃及去。』
verses.en: I have certainly seen the suffering[NOTE:1] of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their groaning, and I have come down to rescue them.[NOTE:2] Now[NOTE:3] come, I will send you to Egypt.’[NOTE:4]
notes: Or “to set them free.”
Grk “And now.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
A quotation from Exod 3:7-8, 10.
This same. The reference to “this one” occurs five times in this speech. It is the way the other speeches in Acts refer to Jesus (e.g., Acts 2:23).
verses.commentary:
7:34 This account is found in Exod. 3:7. For me this verse is so theologically significant for
this reason: YHWH heard their prayers, saw the affliction, and responded. He came down to rescue them,
but notice His rescue was effected through human instrumentality. God sent a reluctant Moses. God has
chosen to deal with humans through humans!

verses.zh: 这摩西就是百姓弃绝说『谁立你作我们的首领和审判官』的；　神却藉那在荆棘中显现之使者的手差派他作首领、作救赎的。
verses.en: This same[NOTE:1] Moses they had rejected, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and judge?’[NOTE:2] God sent as both ruler and deliverer[NOTE:3] through the hand of the angel[NOTE:4] who appeared to him in the bush.
notes: A quotation from Exod 2:14 (see Acts 7:27). God saw Moses very differently than the people of the nation did. The reference to a ruler and a judge suggests that Stephen set up a comparison between Moses and Jesus, but he never finished his speech to make the point. The reader of Acts, however, knowing the other sermons in the book, recognizes that the rejection of Jesus is the counterpoint.
Or “liberator.” The meaning “liberator” for λυτρωτήν (lutrōtēn) is given in L&N 37.129: “a person who liberates or releases others.”

Or simply “through the angel.” Here the “hand” could be understood as a figure for the person or the power of the angel himself. The remark about the angel appearing fits the first century Jewish view that God appears to no one (John 1:14-18; Gal 3:19; Deut 33:2 LXX).

Performing wonders and miraculous signs. Again Moses acted like Jesus. The phrase appears 9 times in Acts (2:19, 22, 43; 4:30; 5:12; 6:8; 7:36; 14:3; 15:12).tn Here the context indicates the miraculous nature of the signs mentioned.
verses.commentary:
7:35 "This Moses whom they disowned" God's people regularly reject God's spokesperson (cf. Acts 7:51-52).
This may even be the purpose of Acts 7:27!

▣ "with the help of the angel who appeared to him in the thorn bush" Again God came to an Israelite
outside the Promised Land. God's activity was not limited to any locality. Much of Israel's history
occurred outside Canaan and before the temple in Jerusalem. All through the Israelites' history God's leaders
were rejected by their peers (cf. Acts 7:9,27-28,35,39). This is a recurrent theme.

This angel is depicted as deity (cf. Exod. 3:2,4). This divine physical manifestation can also
be seen in Gen. 16:7-13; 22:11-15; 31:11,13; 48:15-16; Exod. 13:21; 14:19; Jdgs. 2:1; 6:22-23; 13:3-22;
Zech. 3:1-2. However, it must be stated that "the angel of the Lord" is not always a
divine physical manifestation; sometimes he is just an angel, a messenger, (cf. Gen. 24:7,40; Exod. 23:20-23; 32:34;
Num. 22:22; Judg. 5:23; 2 Sam. 24:16; 1 Chr. 21:15ff; Zech. 1:11; 12-13).

verses.zh: 这人领百姓出来，在埃及，在红海，在旷野，四十年间行了奇事神迹。
verses.en: This man led them out, performing wonders and miraculous signs[NOTE:1] in the land of Egypt,[NOTE:2] at[NOTE:3] the Red Sea, and in the wilderness[NOTE:4] for forty years.
notes: Or simply “in Egypt.” The phrase “the land of” could be omitted as unnecessary or redundant.
Grk “and at,” but καί (kai) has not been translated since English normally uses a coordinating conjunction only between the last two elements in a series of three or more.
Or “desert.”
Grk “to the sons of Israel.”
verses.commentary:
7:36 This is a summary of God's miraculous power (i.e., Moses' staff) through Moses and Aaron.
Israel's rejection of Moses parallels their rejection of Jesus, even in the presence of signs and wonders!

verses.zh: 那曾对以色列人说『　神要从你们弟兄中间给你们兴起一位先知像我』的，就是这位摩西。
verses.en: This is the Moses who said to the Israelites,[NOTE:1] ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.’[NOTE:2]
notes: A quotation from Deut 18:15. This quotation sets up Jesus as the “leader-prophet” like Moses (Acts 3:22; Luke 9:35).
This term, ἐκκλησία (ekklēsia), is a secular use of the term that came to mean “church” in the epistles. Here a reference to an assembly is all that is intended.
verses.commentary:
7:37-38 This is a Messianic quote from Deut. 18:15 (cf. Acts 3:22, where Peter quotes the same prophecy).
Stephen is identifying God's presence during the Exodus and Wilderness Wandering Period as both God's angel and
God's special successor of Moses (i.e., the Messiah, the Prophet). Stephen is not depreciating Moses, but truly listening to Moses!

verses.zh: 这人曾在旷野会中和西奈山上，与那对他说话的天使同在，又与我们的祖宗同在，并且领受活泼的圣言传给我们。
verses.en: This is the man who was in the congregation[NOTE:1] in the wilderness[NOTE:2] with the angel who spoke to him at Mount Sinai, and with our ancestors,[NOTE:3] and he[NOTE:4] received living oracles[NOTE:5] to give to you.[NOTE:6]
notes: Or “desert.”
Or “forefathers”; Grk “fathers.”
Grk “fathers, who.” The relative pronoun was replaced by the pronoun “he” and a new clause introduced by “and” was begun in the translation at this point to improve the English style.
Or “messages.” This is an allusion to the law given to Moses.

‡ The first person pronoun ἡμῖν (hēmin, “to us”) is read by A C D E Ψ 33 1739 M lat sy, while the second person pronoun ὑμῖν (humin, “to you”) is read by P74 א B 36 453 al co. The second person pronoun thus has significantly better external support. As well, ὑμῖν is a harder reading in this context, both because it is surrounded by first person pronouns and because Stephen perhaps “does not wish to disassociate himself from those who received God’s revelation in the past, but only from those who misinterpreted and disobeyed that revelation” (TCGNT 307). At the same time, Stephen does associate himself to some degree with his disobedient ancestors in v. 39, suggesting that the decisive break does not really come until v. 51 (where both his present audience and their ancestors are viewed as rebellious). Thus, both externally and internally ὑμῖν is the preferred reading.
Grk “whom our.” The continuation of the sentence as a relative clause is awkward in English, so a new sentence was started in the translation at this point.
verses.commentary:
7:38 "congregation" This is the Greek term ekklesia, but in this context, it is used in the sense
of "the assembly of Israel," not church.

verses.en: Our[NOTE:1] ancestors[NOTE:2] were unwilling to obey[NOTE:3] him, but pushed him aside[NOTE:4] and turned back to Egypt in their hearts,
notes: Or “forefathers”; Grk “fathers.”
To obey. Again the theme of the speech is noted. The nation disobeyed the way of God and opted for Egypt over the promised land.
Pushed him aside. This is the second time Moses is “pushed aside” in Stephen’s account (see v. 27).
Or simply “of Egypt.” The phrase “the land of” could be omitted as unnecessary or redundant.
verses.commentary:
7:39 "our fathers were unwilling to be obedient to him" Stephen is connecting the dots of OT rebellion.
His implication is that the Jews have always rejected God's leaders, and now they have rejected the Messiah.

▣ "repudiated him" This account is found in Num. 14:3-4.

verses.zh: 对亚伦说：『你且为我们造些神像，在我们前面引路；因为领我们出埃及地的那个摩西，我们不知道他遭了甚么事。』
verses.en: saying to Aaron, ‘Make us gods who will go in front of us, for this Moses, who led us out of the land of Egypt[NOTE:1] —we do not know what has happened to him!’[NOTE:2]
notes: A quotation from Exod 32:1, 23. Doubt (we do not know what has happened to him) expresses itself in unfaithful action. The act is in contrast to God’s promise in Exod 23:20.
Grk “And.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
verses.commentary:
7:40-41 This account is found in Exodus 32. This was not idolatry, but the creation of a physical
image of YHWH, but was used in fertility worship (i.e., "rose up to play," Exod. 32:6,19).

M. R. Vincent, Word Studies in the New Testament, pp. 238-239, lists three
possible Egyptian bull gods.

- at Memphis, a calf god named Apis, who was seen as an intermediary between humans and the gods of Egypt

- at Heliopolis, a bull god named Mnevis, also associated with fertility

- at Hermonthis, a bull god names Buchis was associated with a war deity, Mont

verses.zh: 那时，他们造了一个牛犊，又拿祭物献给那像，欢喜自己手中的工作。
verses.en: At[NOTE:1] that time[NOTE:2] they made an idol in the form of a calf,[NOTE:3] brought[NOTE:4] a sacrifice to the idol, and began rejoicing[NOTE:5] in the works of their hands.[NOTE:6]
notes: Grk “In those days.”
Or “a bull calf” (see Exod 32:4-6). The term μοσχοποιέω (moschopoieō) occurs only in Christian writings according to BDAG 660 s.v.
Grk “and brought,” but καί (kai) has not been translated since English normally uses a coordinating conjunction only between the last two elements in a series of three or more.
The imperfect verb εὐφραίνοντο (euphrainonto) has been translated ingressively. See BDAG 414-15 s.v. εὐφραίνω 2.
Or “in what they had done.”
The expression and gave them over suggests similarities to the judgment on the nations described by Paul in Rom 1:18-32.
verses.commentary:
7:41 Stephen interprets the golden calf as an idol (the temples at Dan and Bethel, cf. 1 Kgs. 12:26-30) and
uses this historical event to introduce a quote from Amos 5, which implies that Israel, even as far back as the Exodus
and Wilderness Wandering, was idolatrous and rebellious.

verses.zh: 神就转脸不顾，任凭他们事奉天上的日月星辰，正如先知书上所写的说：以色列家啊，你们四十年间在旷野，岂是将牺牲和祭物献给我吗？
verses.en: But God turned away from them and gave them over[NOTE:1] to worship the host[NOTE:2] of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘It was not to me that you offered slain animals and sacrifices[NOTE:3] forty years in the wilderness, was it,[NOTE:4] house of Israel?
notes: Or “stars.”sn To worship the hosts of heaven. Their action violated Deut 4:19; 17:2-5. See Ps 106:36-43.
The two terms for sacrifices “semantically reinforce one another and are here combined essentially for emphasis” (L&N 53.20).
The Greek construction anticipates a negative reply which is indicated in the translation by the ‘tag’ question, “was it?”
Or “tent.”sn A tabernacle was a tent used to house religious objects or a shrine (i.e., a portable sanctuary).
verses.commentary:
7:42 "God turned away and delivered them up to serve" Verses 42 and 43 are quotes from Amos 5:25-27
where Amos asserts that Israel was always offering sacrifices to foreign gods. It was a regular, and early,
pattern of their history (cf. Josh. 24:20). This reminds one of the drastic statements of rejection in
Romans 1:24,26,28.

▣ "the host of heaven" This refers to Sumerian, Assyrian, and Babylonian astral worship (cf. Deut. 4:19;
17:3; 2 Kgs. 17:16; 27:3; 2 Chr. 33:3,5; Jer. 8:2; 19:13).

There are several textual problems between the Hebrew text (MT) of Amos 5:25-27, the Greek
text (LXX) and Stephen's quote:

- the name of the star god

- the MT has kywn or kaiwann, the Assyrian name for the planet Saturn

- the LXX has rypn or raiphan, which may be repa, the Egyptian name for the planetary god of Saturn

- the Hebrew text (MT) and the Greek text (LXX) have "beyond Damascus," while Stephen quotes
"beyond Babylon"

There is no known manuscript of Amos that has the reading. Stephen may have been combining the Assyrians
exile, of which Amos speaks, with the later Babylonian exile of Judah, but substituting the place of exile.

The worship of astral deities began in Mesopotamia, but spread into Syria and Canaan (cf. Job 31:26,27). The
archaeological discovery at Tell El-Amarna, which included hundreds of letters from Canaan to Egypt in the 14th century
B. C. also uses these astral deities as place names.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

▣ "in the book of the prophets" This refers to the scroll that contained the twelve minor
prophets (cf. Acts 13:40). The quote in Acts 7:42-43 is from the Septuagint of Amos 5:25-27; see
notes online.

The next phrase in Acts 7:42 is a question that expects a "no" answer.

verses.zh: 你们抬着摩洛的帐幕和理番神的星，就是你们所造为要敬拜的像。因此，我要把你们迁到巴比伦外去。
verses.en: But you took along the tabernacle[NOTE:1] of Moloch[NOTE:2] and the star of the[NOTE:3] god Rephan,[NOTE:4] the images you made to worship, but I will deport[NOTE:5] you beyond Babylon.’[NOTE:6]
notes: Moloch was a Canaanite deity who was believed to be the god of the sky and the sun.

‡ Most mss, including several significant ones (P74 א A C E Ψ 33 1739 M h p vg syh mae bo Cyr), have ὑμῶν (humōn, “your”) here, in conformity with the LXX of Amos 5:26. But other significant and diverse witnesses lack the pronoun: The lack of ὑμῶν in B D 36 453 gig syp sa Irlat Or is difficult to explain if it is not the autographic wording here. NA28 has the word in brackets, indicating some doubt as to its authenticity.

Rephan (῾Ραιφάν, Rhaiphan) was a pagan deity. The term was a name for Saturn. It was variously spelled in the mss (BDAG 903 s.v. has Rompha as an alternate spelling). The references cover a range of deities and a history of unfaithfulness.
Or “I will make you move.”
A quotation from Amos 5:25-27. This constituted a prediction of the exile.
Or “forefathers”; Grk “fathers.”
verses.commentary:
7:43 "Moloch" The Hebrew CONSONANTS for the
word "king" are mlk (BDB 574). There are several Canaanite gods whose names are a play on these
three CONSONANTS, Milcom, Molech, or Moloch. Moloch was
the chief fertility god of the Amorites to whom children were offered to ensure the health and prosperity of the
community or nation (cf. Lev. 20:2-5; Deut. 12:31; 1 Kgs. 11:5,7,33; 2 Kgs. 23:10,13,14; Jer. 7:31; 32:35).
A. T. Robertson, Word Pictures In the New Testament, vol. 3, p. 93, says Moloch was "an ox-headed
image with arms outstretched in which children were placed and hollow underneath so that fire could burn underneath."

The mention of the term Molech in Lev. 18:21 in context of inappropriate sexual unions, has caused
some scholars to assume that children were not sacrificed to Molech, but dedicated to him as temple prostitutes, male
and female. The concept fits in the general practices of fertility worship.

was depicted as a bull head representing "Horus, the bull."

The other option is that it depicted the Roman god Osiris. But it must be admitted there is much confusion
in trying to understand and identify Egyptian deities!

verses.zh: 大卫在　神面前蒙恩，祈求为雅各的　神预备居所；
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] found favor[NOTE:2] with[NOTE:3] God and asked that he could[NOTE:4] find a dwelling place[NOTE:5] for the house[NOTE:6] of Jacob.
notes: Or “grace.”
Grk “before,” “in the presence of.”

The words “that he could” are not in the Greek text, but are implied as the (understood) subject of the infinitive εὑρεῖν (heurein). This understands David’s request as asking that he might find the dwelling place. The other possibility would be to supply “that God” as the subject of the infinitive: “and asked that God find a dwelling place.” Unfortunately this problem is complicated by the extremely difficult problem with the Greek text in the following phrase (“house of Jacob” vs. “God of Jacob”).
On this term see BDAG 929 s.v. σκήνωμα a (Ps 132:5).

Some mss read θεῷ (theō, “God”) here, a variant much easier to understand in the context. The reading “God” is supported by א2 A C E Ψ 33 1739 M lat sy co. The more difficult οἴκῳ (oikō, “house”) is supported by P74 א* B D H 049. Thus the second reading is preferred both externally because of better ms evidence and internally because it is hard to see how a copyist finding the reading “God” would change it to “house,” while it is easy to see how (given the LXX of Ps 132:5) a copyist might assimilate the reading and change “house” to “God.” However, some scholars think the reading “house” is so difficult as to be unacceptable. Others (like Lachmann and Hort) resorted to conjectural emendation at this point. Others (Ropes) sought an answer in an underlying Aramaic expression. Not everyone thinks the reading “house” is too difficult to be accepted as original (see Lake and Cadbury). A. F. J. Klijn, “Stephen’s Speech—Acts vii.2-53, ” NTS 4 (1957): 25-31, compared the idea of a “house within the house of Israel” with the Manual of Discipline from Qumran, a possible parallel that seems to support the reading “house” as authentic. (For the more detailed discussion from which this note was derived, see TCGNT 308-9.)
See 1 Kgs 8:1-21.
verses.commentary:

Do these verses imply an argument for the inclusion of Gentiles? If so, it seems somewhat

It was the Greek-speaking Jews (i.e., the Seven in Acts 6) who saw and proclaimed the worldwide mission even

verses.en: You[NOTE:1] received the law by decrees given by angels,[NOTE:2] but you did not obey[NOTE:3] it.”
notes: Decrees given by angels. According to Jewish traditions in the first century, the law of Moses was mediated through angels. See also the note on “angel” in 7:35.tn Traditionally, “as ordained by angels,” but εἰς (eis) with the accusative here should be understood as instrumental (a substitute for ἐν [en]); so BDAG 291 s.v. εἰς 9, BDF §206. Thus the phrase literally means “received the law by the decrees [orders] of angels” with the genitive understood as a subjective genitive, that is, the angels gave the decrees.
The Greek word φυλάσσω (phulassō, traditionally translated “keep”) in this context connotes preservation of and devotion to an object as well as obedience.
This verb, which also occurs in Acts 5:33, means “cut to the quick” or “deeply infuriated” (BDAG 235 s.v. διαπρίω).
verses.commentary:

Septuagint in which God gave the law to Moses through angelic mediation which seems to be confirmed by

▣ "yet did not keep it" Stephen opened his defense with "hear" (BDB 1033) which may reflect the

both assert "be doers of the word not merely hearers" (cf. James 1:22-23 following Jesus, Matt. 7:24-27;
Luke 11:48; John 13:17; as did Paul, Rom. 2:13).

verses.en: But Stephen,[NOTE:1] full[NOTE:2] of the Holy Spirit, looked intently[NOTE:3] toward heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing[NOTE:4] at the right hand of God.
notes: Grk “being full,” but the participle ὑπάρχων (huparchōn) has not been translated since it would be redundant in English.
Grk “looking intently toward heaven, saw.” The participle ἀτενίσας (atenisas) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

The picture of Jesus standing (rather than seated) probably indicates his rising to receive his child. By announcing his vision, Stephen thoroughly offended his audience, who believed no one could share God’s place in heaven. The phrase is a variation on Ps 110:1.

Grk “And he said, ‘Look!’” Because of the length of the Greek sentence and the tendency of contemporary English style to use shorter sentences, καί (kai) has not been translated here; a new sentence is begun instead.

7:55 "Holy Spirit. . .God. . .Jesus" Notice the mention of the Triune God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TRINITY

▣ "Being full of the Holy Spirit" The concept of being filled with the Spirit for proclamation
of the gospel is unique to Acts (i.e., plēroō, cf. Acts 2:4; 4:8,31; plērēs,
cf. Acts 6:3,5,8; 7:55; 11:24). See full note at Acts 5:17.

The biblical truths related to the Spirit are characterized as:

- the person of the Spirit (cf. John 14-16; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PERSONHOOD OF THE SPIRIT)

- the baptism of the Spirit (cf. 1 Cor. 12:13; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: BAPTISM OF THE SPIRIT)

- the fruit of the Spirit (cf. Gal. 5:22-23)

- the gifts of the Spirit (cf. 1 Corinthians 12; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT [gift of])

- the filling of the Spirit (cf. Eph. 5:18; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT (filling))

Of all of these, Acts focuses on #5. The early church leaders were empowered, apparently
again and again, to boldly and powerfully proclaim the gospel of Jesus Christ. In Stephen's case the
effectiveness of his sermon cost him his life.

▣ "gazed intently" Luke is very fond of this term (cf. Luke 4:20; 22:56; Acts 1:10; 3:4,12;
6:15; 7:55; 10:4; 11:6; 13:9; 14:9; 23:1). Stephen looked up, as was typical of the Jewish manner of prayer,
but instead of a physical posture for praying, God allowed him to see into heaven itself.

▣ "saw the glory of God" Abraham saw this same "God of glory" in Acts 7:2. Notice that Stephen is
not said to have seen God, but His glory. No one could see God and live (see full note online at Exod. 33:17-23). Job
believed he would see God (cf. Job 19:25-27; Acts 7:55). Jesus promises that one day the pure in heart will see God (cf. Matt. 5:8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CAN HUMANS SEE GOD AND LIVE?

▣ "Jesus standing at the right hand of God" Jesus being at God's right hand is an anthropomorphic
idiom for the place of divine power and authority (i.e., Acts 2:32-33; 3:21; 5:31; 13:33). The fact that Jesus was
standing shows His interest and care for the first Christian martyr.

God revealed Himself to Stephen in the form and manner that Stephen could receive (i.e., a variation of
Ps. 110:1). This does not mean to imply

- that heaven is "up"

- that God is sitting on a throne

It does mean to convey Jesus' care and concern. We must be careful of culturally conditioned
anthropomorphic language as the source of doctrine. Modern western readers' trying to take every passage
literally as a way to show trust or devotion to the Bible is an unfortunate cultural trend. God truly
reveals Himself to His creation, but He does so in earthly ways and forms in which they can understand.
There is surely an element of accommodation. Fallen, finite, human creatures are not able to fully comprehend
the spiritual realm. God chooses things in our cultural and experiential world to use as analogies and
imagery to communicate to us. These are surely true, but not exhaustive.

verses.zh: 就说：「我看见天开了，人子站在　神的右边。」
verses.en: “Look!” he said.[NOTE:1] “I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!”
notes: They covered their ears to avoid hearing what they considered to be blasphemy.
verses.commentary:
7:56 "Son of Man" Stephen obviously is identifying Jesus with the "Righteous One" of Acts 5:52. His
hearers would not have missed this Messianic affirmation. The title "son of man" has two OT usages:

- it was a common phrase for a person (i.e., Ezek. 2:1; Ps. 8:4)

- it was used of the divine personage (i.e., Messiah) in Daniel 7:13-14; Ps. 110:1; Mark 13:26; 14:62

Therefore, based on Daniel 7, it had connotations of both humanity and deity. This is why Jesus used it as a
self-designation and also because it was not used by the rabbis who tended to use OT titles in exclusivistic,
nationalistic, and militaristic ways. This reference by Stephen is the only one to use this phrase outside of the
words of Jesus (cf. John 12:34).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

verses.zh: 众人大声喊叫，捂着耳朵，齐心拥上前去，
verses.en: But they covered their ears,[NOTE:1] shouting out with a loud voice, and rushed at him with one intent.
notes: Grk “And when.” Because of the length of the Greek sentence and the tendency of contemporary English style to use shorter sentences, καί (kai) has not been translated here; a new sentence is begun instead.
verses.commentary:
7:57-58 These hearers believed that Stephen had blasphemed by asserting that Jesus was the coming
Son of Man (cf. Dan. 7:13). For these monotheistic Jews this was just too much! They did to Stephen what
Moses mandated for blasphemy (cf. Lev. 24:14-16; Deut. 13:9; 17:7). Stephen's affirmation is either true
or he is a blasphemer worthy of death! There can be no middle ground about the claims of Jesus
(cf. John 14:6-9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

7:57 "rushed at him with one impulse" This is the very term used so often by Luke to describe the
unity of the early disciples (cf. Acts 1:14; 2:46; 5:12; 15:25). The Sanhedrin was unified in their anger
and rejection of Stephen (also see Acts 18:12, where the Jews of Achaia reject Paul and Acts 19:29 of the anger
of the pagans of Ephesus against Christians).

verses.zh: 把他推到城外，用石头打他。作见证的人把衣裳放在一个少年人名叫扫罗的脚前。
verses.en: When[NOTE:1] they had driven him out of the city, they began to stone him,[NOTE:2] and the witnesses laid their cloaks[NOTE:3] at the feet of a young man named Saul.
notes: They began to stone him. The irony of the scene is that the people do exactly what the speech complains about in v. 52.
Or “outer garments.”sn Laid their cloaks. The outer garment, or cloak, was taken off and laid aside to leave the arms free (in this case for throwing stones).

Grk “And they.” Because of the length of the Greek sentence and the tendency of contemporary English style to use shorter sentences, καί (kai) has not been translated here; a new sentence is begun instead.
verses.commentary:
7:58 "driven him out of the city" No one could be killed inside Jerusalem because it was "holy" ground!

▣ "stoning him" It is often stated that the Jews under Roman occupation did not have the
right of capital punishment. This shows that that is not always true. Mob violence could not be stopped
quickly.

SPECIAL TOPIC: STONE TO DEATH

▣ "a young man named Saul" In Jewish circles, one was considered young up to age 40. This is our
first encounter with Saul of Tarsus by name, later to become Paul the Apostle. Paul heard Stephen's OT
survey and possibly had heard him earlier in the synagogue of the Cilicians in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9). One
wonders whether this began Saul's period of doubt, which he tried to deal with by persecuting Christians.

verses.zh: 他们正用石头打的时候，司提反呼吁主说：「求主耶稣接收我的灵魂！」
verses.en: They[NOTE:1] continued to stone Stephen while he prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!”
notes: Grk “Then falling to his knees he cried out.” The participle θείς (theis) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
verses.commentary:
7:59 "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" This is an AORIST MIDDLE IMPERATIVE. Notice that
Stephen believed that he was going to heaven to be with Jesus (cf. 2 Cor. 5:6,8) and not to hades (i.e.,
the holding place of the dead like the Hebrew sheol). Stephen may have witnessed Jesus' crucifixion,
or at least had heard about it in detail because he uses two similar phrases (i.e., Acts 7:59 and 60,
cf. Luke 23:34,46).

It is interesting to note that Stephen prays to Jesus, as did the disciples in Acts 1:24.
However, in the rest of the NT prayer is made to the Father in the name of the Son.

verses.commentary:
7:60 "falling on his knees" Stoning was not always a quick experience. The text implies it took
several minutes.

▣ "he cried out with a loud voice" This also mimics Jesus' experience. These words were as
much for the crowd as for YHWH. These words must have echoed in Saul's ears.

▣ "he fell asleep" This is biblical imagery for physical death (ex. Job 3:13; 14:12; Ps. 76:5;
2 Sam. 7:12; 1 Kgs. 2:10; Jer. 51:39,57; Dan. 12:2; Matt. 27:52; John 11:11; Acts 7:60; 13:36;
1 Cor. 15:6,18,20; 1 Thess. 4:13; 2 Pet. 3:4). This does not affirm the doctrine of "soul-sleep."

- How was Jesus like Moses, Acts 7:37?

- What was so significant about Stephen's vision of Jesus?

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS TO ACTS 7

- Stephen's speech in Acts 7 is the longest recorded sermon in Acts. It breaks the theological
ground for Paul's (and the church's) understanding of the gospel's relationship to the Old Testament.
Stephen's sermon answers the charges made against him, showing that

- God has often acted outside of Israel and the temple

- Mesopotamia

- Egypt

- Midian

- God has always worked with Gentiles

- Israelites/Jews have always rejected YHWH's message and spokesmen, and now they have rejected His Messiah!

- Stephen's defense affected Saul of Tarsus' heart and later his theology.

- Stephen reveals the continuing covenant infidelity of the Jewish people and God's revelations outside the
Promised Land and apart from the temple in Jerusalem, which had become the focus of first century Jewish
worship (see Jeremiah's sermon in Jeremiah 7).

- The Jewish people had regularly rejected God's spokesman and now they did it again. They had violently
rejected Jesus of Nazareth and they were about to violently reject Stephen, His witness.

- Stephen is charged by the same group with similar charges of blasphemy as Jesus was. As he was
being stoned, Stephen said several things which mimic Jesus' words and actions on the cross.

- Stephen's perspective on the relationship between Jews and Christians will set the stage for the
persecution (cf. Acts 8:1-3) and ultimate splitting (i.e., Pharisaical deliberations at Jamnia in A.D. 90
which led to the Eighteen Benedictions, curse formulas) of these two groups. It is surely possible that God used Stephen,
as He did Samson in the OT, to start a fight thereby forcing the spread of the gospel beyond Palestine.

- Stephen's speech/defense/sermon has several details which differ from the Hebrew OT (he quotes
from the Septuagint). Should scholars try to defend Stephen's sayings or allow them to be Jewish traditions
or even historical errors (e.g., lists of things in the Ark between OT and Hebrews)? This question reveals the emotional
and intellectual biases of interpreters. I believe that the Bible is true history, that Christianity stands or falls on the events
of the Bible. However, the very beginning of the Bible (i.e., Genesis 1-11) and the end of the Bible (i.e., book of Revelation)
are not "typical history"! As for the intervening accounts, I think they are accurate and true (cf. 2 Tim. 3:15-17). This takes
into account that sometimes there are:

- differences in numbers

- differences in genre

- differences in details

- rabbinical techniques of interpretation (ex. combining two or more texts)

- please see note at Rom. 9:33 about Paul's typological use of the OT

These do not affect my affirmation of the historical accuracy or trustworthiness of biblical narratives.
Stephen may have been recounting what he learned in Synagogue school or he may have modified texts to fit
his purpose (as Paul does in Eph. 4:8)! To miss his message by focusing on one or two details shows our modern sense
of historiography (i.e., cause and effect, chronological) and not the first century's sense of history (i.e., theological purpose). See
John H. Walton and D. Brent Sandy, The Lost World of Scripture, which documents how oral cultures pass on their traditions.
